newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Firms satisfied with HK tax system -- Coopers poll.
newsitem.headline: Firms satisfied with HK tax system -- Coopers poll.

text.p: Most of the companies polled by Coopers & Lybrand (CL) in Hong Kong said they were satisfied with the Hong Kong tax system and had few anxieties about the future after the British colony reverts to China this year.

"In terms of our position in Asia Pacific region, again the survey results indicated that Hong Kong is still by a long way the preferred location for business executives," Tim Lui, a senior tax partner at CL said.
The survey, conducted in January of 125 companies ranging from multinationals to Hong Kong-listed and private companies, revealed some concern about Hong Kong's high costs.
However, 84 percent of respondents voted Hong Kong's tax system as the most attractive in the region.
A total of 98 percent of the companies polled rated the tax system as excellent or very good.
They said the simplicity of Hong Kong's tax system combined with the low tax rate was key to its attractiveness.
About one-quarter of the respondents expected any changes to be made to the tax system after Britain handed the territory back to China on July 1.
Multinationals, concerned with the high cost of doing business in Hong Kong, said regional headquarters were the most deserving cause for tax incentives, it said.
High technology and manufacturing industries were also concerned about the high costs associated with doing business in Hong Kong.
Coopers said respondents proposed only minor changes to the tax system for the fiscal year 1997/98 ending March 31.
Financial Secretary Donald Tsang is expected to give the 1997/98 budget speech next month for the year straddling the handover of Hong Kong.
They suggested the introduction of group relief for companies owned substantially by the same shareholders.
Currently, tax is payable by profitable group companies but no relief is available for tax losess incurred in the same year by other group companies, the consultancy said.
Coopers said respondents wanted to see the complete abolition of estate duty, minor adjustments in stamp duties, and increases not exceeding the inflation rate for other duties and charges.
It suggested personal tax allowances be increased at a small margin above inflation.
